Wind power’s prominence in Europe brings increased vulnerabilities to seabed cable damage, as offshore wind generation depends on subsea cables to transmit electricity from turbines to shore (see Section 2.3). (see Figure D-3), a coordinated attack during a conflict could reduce power to the European theater precisely when operations require more from local grids. In the past 18 months, the Gulf of Finland has seen two undersea cable damage incidents, and the Baltic Sea region has reported at least six suspected sabotage events since 2022 (Jack, Mackenzie, and Clark 2025). In February 2023, Dutch military intelligence issued a warning about Russia’s reported efforts to survey offshore wind plants and disrupt critical infrastructure in the North Sea (Cooper 2023). This vulnerability will likely increase as Europe becomes more dependent on offshore wind to meet electricity demand (see Figure D-4). Offshore wind installations are projected to surpass 10 GW in 2028 and 20 GW in 2030 (Statista 2024). Wind is Germany’s primary source of electricity (Farhat and Wertz 2025), and the country installed 4.0 GW of new capacity in 2024, 18% of which came from offshore wind. This brought their total installed capacity to 72.7 GW, making it the largest wind fleet in Europe (Costanzo and Brindley 2024). Figure D-3. European offshore wind plants map. Source: Telsnig 2021; European Commission 2021 D.3 Operational and Logistical Challenges The rapid adoption of advanced energy technologies in Europe could strain DOW readiness in times of surge energy needs, especially as infrastructure shifts away from legacy systems (see Section 4.3), such as gas stations in favor of electric vehicle (EV) charging (Consultancy.eu 2024). Fossil fuel generation fell by 75 TWh (9%) from 2023, reaching its lowest level in more than 40 years (Rosslowe and Petrovich 2025), signaling shrinking infrastructure tied to these industries. Moreover, many NATO militaries, some with commitments to achieve net zero by 2050, have more aggressive advanced energy technology adoption plans than DOW, potentially leading to disagreements regarding interoperability and strategic planning for operational readiness (Griffiths, Hammock, and Tate 2025). This could challenge a unified approach to efforts such as the 2023 NATO Climate Change and Security Impact Assessment’s emphasis on the need to research alternative fuels for NATO warships—or choosing among focusing on securing the carbon-based liquid fuel supply chain, investing in electrifying the force while relying on Europe’s increasing wind and solar sectors, or prioritizing the development of nuclear capabilities (Griffiths, Hammock, and Tate 2025).
